steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI paper presenting ABScribe, a writing interface for exploring and organizing multiple writing variations when co-writing with LLMs. Cover why revision matters, what current tools and LLM interfaces lack, related HCI work, the design of ABScribe, and our user study and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Revision is essential: iterative, granular, non-linear
- Current writing interfaces are linear; value of multiple variations
- LLMs make variations easy to generate but hard to manage
- Related HCI work on LLM tools
- ABScribe and its five interface elements
- Evaluation study and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Revision
  - essential to writing (cite)
  - professional writers rewrite hundreds of times (cite); recommend rewriting as core strategy (cite)
  - beyond minor edits: rework ideas, affect knowledge (cite); explore alternative variations for line of argument (cite)
  - iterative (cite): repeated cycles; granular (cite): word/sentence/paragraph; non-linear (cite): reconsider variations throughout
- Current interfaces
  - linear revision history (Google docs, Microsoft Word)
  - iterative, granular edits ok; hard to consider multiple variations at once and organize without replacing text or cluttering doc (pasting in sequence)
  - HCI/design: multiple (at least 5) variations -> better ideas (cite), avoid fixation (cite)
  - hypothesis: applies to writing, given support with minimal workload
- LLMs
  - ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM 2, LLaMA 2, Gemini (cite each)
  - generate multiple variations via natural language prompting (cite) -> less workload
  - but harder to organize, compare, modify with chat-based / in-place editing; variations lost in linear chat histories, stored as comments or in-line blocks
  - easier to generate -> harder to manage
- Related HCI work
  - focus on prompt engineering (cite) and generative capabilities (cite)
  - Zamfirescu-Pereira et al.: helping non-AI experts craft prompts
  - Dang et al. (cite): users prefer choosing from multiple suggestions, using draft content over external prompts (more effort)
  - Yuan et al (cite): creative writing; output need not be perfect to be useful
  - useful even if heavily revised or not used in final draft (cite)
  - -> value of affordances for managing imperfect AI variations
- ABScribe
  - novel interface: rapid exploration/organization of multiple variations in LLM-based human-AI co-writing
  - inspired by Kim et al. framework: object-oriented interactions with LLMs (cite)
  - five elements: (i) Variation Fields; (ii) Popup Toolbar (hover to reveal variations); (iii) Variation Sidebar (accordion UI); (iv) AI Modifiers (reusable LLM instruction buttons); (v) AI Drafter (insert LLM text) (Figure 1)
- Evaluation and contributions
  - controlled study, revision tasks + interviews, 12 writers
  - baseline: GPT-4-based AI integrated rich text editor + chat-based assistant
  - lower subjective task workload (d=1.20,p<0.001,); better perceptions of revision process (d=2.\text{41},p<0.001)
  - (1) design + implementation, open source on GitHub
  - (2) 12-participant study results; user perspectives on linear vs non-linear revision

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Revision is essential to the writing process. Professional writers often write and rewrite text hundreds of times, and they recommend rewriting as a core strategy for writing well. Effective revision is more than minor editorial changes; it can help writers rework ideas and powerfully affect their knowledge when they explore alternative variations to find a line of argument. The revision process is iterative, meaning it happens in repeated cycles throughout writing; it is granular, meaning it happens at the word, sentence, or paragraph-level; and it is non-linear, meaning it requires constantly reconsidering potential variations of existing text throughout the passage.

Current writing interfaces mostly do not support a non-linear revision process and mainly support linear representations of revision history (e.g., revision history in popular word processing software like Google docs or Microsoft Word). These tools do support iterative and granular edits, but it is still hard for writers to consider multiple writing variations at the same time and organize them without replacing earlier text, or without cluttering documents when they end up pasting them in sequence. Insights from HCI and traditional design practice suggest that considering multiple (at least 5) variations at the same time can lead to better ideas and avoid fixation. We hypothesize that this may also apply to writing, if writers get adequate support in managing multiple variations with minimal workload.

Advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM 2, LLaMA 2, and Gemini can let writers generate multiple variations of text through natural language prompting, which could reduce the workload of generating text variations. But easier generation can make the challenges around systematically organizing, comparing, and modifying multiple variations worse with existing chat-based and in-place editing interfaces, where users have to find text variations in linear chat histories and store them in their document as comments or separate in-line text blocks. When text variations become easier to generate with AI, they become harder to manage.

- Related HCI work
  - focus on prompt engineering (cite) and generative capabilities (cite)
  - Zamfirescu-Pereira et al.: helping non-AI experts craft prompts
  - Dang et al. (cite): users prefer choosing from multiple suggestions, using draft content over external prompts (more effort)
  - Yuan et al (cite): creative writing; output need not be perfect to be useful
  - useful even if heavily revised or not used in final draft (cite)
  - -> value of affordances for managing imperfect AI variations
- ABScribe
  - novel interface: rapid exploration/organization of multiple variations in LLM-based human-AI co-writing
  - inspired by Kim et al. framework: object-oriented interactions with LLMs (cite)
  - five elements: (i) Variation Fields; (ii) Popup Toolbar (hover to reveal variations); (iii) Variation Sidebar (accordion UI); (iv) AI Modifiers (reusable LLM instruction buttons); (v) AI Drafter (insert LLM text) (Figure 1)
- Evaluation and contributions
  - controlled study, revision tasks + interviews, 12 writers
  - baseline: GPT-4-based AI integrated rich text editor + chat-based assistant
  - lower subjective task workload (d=1.20,p<0.001,); better perceptions of revision process (d=2.\text{41},p<0.001)
  - (1) design + implementation, open source on GitHub
  - (2) 12-participant study results; user perspectives on linear vs non-linear revision

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Revision is essential to the writing process. Professional writers often write and rewrite text hundreds of times, and they recommend rewriting as a core strategy for writing well. Effective revision is more than minor editorial changes; it can help writers rework ideas and powerfully affect their knowledge when they explore alternative variations to find a line of argument. The revision process is iterative, meaning it happens in repeated cycles throughout writing; it is granular, meaning it happens at the word, sentence, or paragraph-level; and it is non-linear, meaning it requires constantly reconsidering potential variations of existing text throughout the passage.

Current writing interfaces mostly do not support a non-linear revision process and mainly support linear representations of revision history (e.g., revision history in popular word processing software like Google docs or Microsoft Word). These tools do support iterative and granular edits, but it is still hard for writers to consider multiple writing variations at the same time and organize them without replacing earlier text, or without cluttering documents when they end up pasting them in sequence. Insights from HCI and traditional design practice suggest that considering multiple (at least 5) variations at the same time can lead to better ideas and avoid fixation. We hypothesize that this may also apply to writing, if writers get adequate support in managing multiple variations with minimal workload.

Advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM 2, LLaMA 2, and Gemini can let writers generate multiple variations of text through natural language prompting, which could reduce the workload of generating text variations. But easier generation can make the challenges around systematically organizing, comparing, and modifying multiple variations worse with existing chat-based and in-place editing interfaces, where users have to find text variations in linear chat histories and store them in their document as comments or separate in-line text blocks. When text variations become easier to generate with AI, they become harder to manage.

Recent HCI studies on designing LLM-based tools have mostly focused on prompt engineering and on exploring the generative capabilities of LLMs. For example, Zamfirescu-Pereira et al. investigated ways to help non-AI experts craft effective prompts, and Dang et al. found that users preferred to choose from multiple suggestions and to use content from the draft to guide LLM usage, rather than writing external prompts, which take more effort. Yuan et al, explored how users might use LLMs for creative writing and found that the model output did not have to be perfect to be useful to users. Many users found the output useful even when they had to revise the text a lot or decided not to put it in their final draft. This shows the potential value of designing affordances that help manage imperfect AI-generated variations. Even if these variations don't end up in the final text, they might still be worth considering.

In this paper we present ABScribe, a novel writing interface that supports rapidly exploring and organizing multiple writing variations in LLM-based human-AI co-writing tasks. We take inspiration from a design framework by Kim et al. that shows the potential of object-oriented interactions with LLMs for encouraging iteration and experimentation during writing, and we propose an ensemble of five interface elements that help writers work swiftly with multiple writing variations: (i) Variation Fields, which store multiple human and AI-generated variations inside flexible text segments in a non-linear way, without overwriting text; (ii) the Popup Toolbar, which reveals the corresponding variations inside a Variation Field when users hover their mouse over buttons that represent each variation, so they can compare rapidly without breaking text flow; (iii) the Variation Sidebar, which organizes all the variations in a navigable format inside an accordion UI; (iv) AI Modifiers, which automatically encapsulate LLM instructions into reusable buttons that can be applied across different Variation Fields; and (v) the AI Drafter, which lets writers insert LLM-generated text directly into the document (see Figure 1).

To validate our design, we ran a controlled evaluation study with revision tasks and interviews with 12 writers. It compared ABScribe with a widely-used baseline workflow, which consists of an AI integrated rich text editor based on GPT-4 together with a chat-based conversational AI assistant. Our findings show that compared to the baseline, ABScribe significantly reduces subjective task workload (d=1.20,p<0.001,), and improves user perceptions of the revision process (d=2.\text{41},p<0.001). Our key contributions are:

- (1) The design and implementation of ABScribe, an LLM-enhanced writing interface which supports rapid exploration and organization of multiple text variations in human-AI co-writing tasks. We have made all the code for ABScribe open source and available on GitHub.

- (2) The results of a 12-participant user study with writers, which demonstrate the efficacy of the ABScribe interface ensemble and its advantages over a commonly used baseline workflow, and user perspectives on how writers explore multiple variations in human-AI co-writing tasks using a linear and a non-linear revision process.

Effective revision goes beyond minor editorial changes, and may help writers rework ideas and powerfully affect their knowledge [7,5] as they explore alternative variations to find a line of argument [7]. The revision process is iterative [8,7]: it happens in repeated cycles throughout the writing process; granular [9,4]: it happens at the word, sentence, or paragraph-level; and non-linear [10,5]: it requires constant reconsideration of potential variations of existing text throughout the passage.

Current writing interfaces tend not to support a non-linear revision process and predominantly support linear representations of revision history (e.g., revision history in popular word processing software such as Google docs or Microsoft Word). While these tools support iterative and granular edits, it remains difficult for writers to simultaneously consider multiple writing variations and to organize them without replacing earlier text, or cluttering documents when they resort to pasting them in sequence. Insights from HCI and traditional design practice suggest that simultaneous consideration of multiple (at least 5) variations can lead to better ideas [11] and avoid fixation [12,11,13,14]. We hypothesize that this may also apply to writing, provided that writers are given adequate support in managing multiple variations with minimal workload.

Advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT [15], GPT-4 [16], PaLM 2 [17], LLaMA 2 [18], and Gemini [19] can enable writers to generate multiple variations of text via natural language prompting [20,21,22,23], potentially reducing the workload of generating text variations. However, easier generation can exacerbate the challenges of systematically organizing, comparing, and modifying multiple variations with existing chat-based and in-place editing interfaces, where users must find text variations in linear chat histories and store them in their document as comments or separate in-line text blocks. As text variations become easier to generate using AI, they become harder to manage.

Recent HCI studies on LLM-based tool design have mainly focused on prompt engineering [24,25,26,27,28,29] and exploring the generative capabilities of LLMs [30,31,32,33,34]. For example, Zamfirescu-Pereira et al. investigated ways to support non-AI experts in crafting effective prompts, and Dang et al. [29] found that users preferred choosing from multiple suggestions and using content from the draft to guide LLM usage over writing external prompts, which require more effort. Yuan et al, [30] explored how users might use LLMs for creative writing and found that the model's output did not need to be perfect to be useful to users. Many users found the output useful even if they had to significantly revise the text or chose not to incorporate it into their final draft [30]. This highlights the potential value of designing affordances that help manage imperfect AI-generated variations. Even if these variations don’t make it into the final text, they might still be valuable to consider.

In this paper, we present ABScribe, a novel writing interface that supports the rapid exploration and organization of multiple writing variations in LLM-based human-AI co-writing tasks. Drawing inspiration from a design framework by Kim et al. which shows the potential for object-oriented interactions with LLMs to encourage iteration and experimentation during writing [35], we propose an ensemble of five interface elements that support writers in swiftly working with multiple writing variations: (i) Variation Fields that store multiple human and AI-generated variations within flexible text segments in a non-linear manner, without overwriting text; (ii) the Popup Toolbar that reveals the corresponding variations inside a Variation Field when users hover over buttons representing each variation, allowing rapid comparisons without breaking text flow; (iii) the Variation Sidebar that organizes all variations in a navigable format within an accordion UI; (iv) AI Modifiers that automatically encapsulate LLM instructions into reusable buttons that can be applied across different Variation Fields; and (v) the AI Drafter which allows writers to insert LLM-generated text directly into the document (see Figure 1).

To validate our design, we conducted a controlled evaluation study involving revision tasks and interviews with 12 writers, comparing ABScribe with a widely-used baseline workflow consisting of an AI integrated rich text editor based on GPT-4 and a chat-based conversational AI assistant. Our findings demonstrate that ABScribe significantly reduces subjective task workload (d=1.20,p<0.001,) and enhances user perceptions of the revision process (d=2.\text{41},p<0.001) compared to the baseline. The key contributions of our work are as follows:

- (1) The design and implementation of ABScribe, an LLM-enhanced writing interface that supports the rapid exploration and organization of multiple text variations in human-AI co-writing tasks. We have made the full code for ABScribe open source and accessible via GitHub.

- (2) The results of a 12-participant user study with writers demonstrating the efficacy of the ABScribe interface ensemble and its advantages over a commonly used baseline workflow, and user perspectives on how writers explore multiple variations in human-AI co-writing tasks using a linear and non-linear revision process.
